prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: Mutations in the ALMS1 gene are the cause of Alström syndrome, a human ciliopathy.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The ALMS1 protein is located at the proximal end of centrioles, suggesting it may affect cilia through a unique mechanism.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: In the absence of ALMS1, centrioles become shorter and often fracture at their proximal ends.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Centrioles lacking ALMS1 show decreased microtubule-organizing activity and damaged centriole linkers.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The transport of Golgi-derived cargo, including transition zone components, to the centrosome is impaired when ALMS1 is missing.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: ALMS1 plays a key role in assembling the transition zone, forming cilia, and regulating the composition of the ciliary membrane.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: In mice, disrupting ALMS1 leads to a progressive, age-dependent loss of cilia in the retina, kidney, and brain.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The authors conclude that Alström syndrome results from disrupted proximal centriole integrity and impaired protein trafficking to the centrosome, which compromises ciliary assembly and maintenance.
facts.subject: humans
